assertions.notes: Explains that by default pasted text arrives as typed characters, with each newline read as KeyCode::Enter, and names bracketed paste (ESC[200~ markers) as the missing mode.
Shows execute!(..., EnableBracketedPaste) and an Event::Paste handler, and says the app must turn it on because ratatui::init() does not.
Requires a rule for multi-line pastes (join, multi-line badge with script execution, or confirm) via sanitize_paste, and states a paste never submits; only a real Enter does.
Calls DisableBracketedPaste in restore_terminal and in a panic hook, and notes ratatui::restore() handles only raw mode and the alternate screen.

The answer says that with bracketed paste off, pasted text arrives as individual keystrokes and each newline becomes `\r`, which crossterm reads as `KeyCode::Enter`. It names the `ESC[200~` wrapping but not 'mode 2004' explicitly.
It enables `EnableBracketedPaste` through crossterm `execute!` and handles `Event::Paste(String)`. It notes that `ratatui::init()` does not enable bracketed paste, so you must add it yourself.

It lists explicit policies: newline markers plus a warning (recommended as safest), joining lines, or rejecting/confirming multi-line pastes. It states a paste should never trigger a submit by itself.

It says to disable bracketed paste on every exit path including panics, and to add `DisableBracketedPaste` to the panic hook because `ratatui::restore()` does not handle it. It also describes the `^[[200~` leftover symptom.
The answer explains that with bracketed paste off, pasted text arrives as individual key events and each newline becomes KeyCode::Enter, which submits the command.
The answer enables EnableBracketedPaste and handles Event::Paste, but never says that crossterm and Ratatui leave bracketed paste off by default.
The answer requires choosing a multi-line policy (join, switch to a multi-line editor, or confirm), recommends one, and says Event::Paste must insert text and never submit.
The answer disables bracketed paste on normal exit and in the panic hook, but does not cover error exit paths or mention that Ratatui's restore() does not undo bracketed paste.
Names Synchronized Output mode 2026 and explains wrapping each frame in CSI ? 2026 h / l so the terminal shows it all at once.
States Ratatui's draw() does not add the markers and wraps draw with crossterm's BeginSynchronizedUpdate/EndSynchronizedUpdate.
Says to always send the end marker even when draw errors, and in the panic hook; the code does this and notes terminals otherwise wait for a timeout.
Describes DECRQM detection (CSI ? 2026 $ p) and fallbacks: a buffered stdout so frames go out in few writes, and preserving Ratatui's diffing so only changed cells are sent.
The answer names synchronized output, DEC mode 2026, and wraps each draw between the CSI ? 2026 h and l sequences so the frame appears at once.

The answer does show calling crossterm's BeginSynchronizedUpdate/EndSynchronizedUpdate, but it says recent Ratatui versions may do this automatically, which contradicts the point that Ratatui does not wrap draws.
The answer says to always send the end sequence on error paths, places res? after End, suggests a Drop guard and the panic hook, and warns that the terminal otherwise stalls until its timeout.

The answer explains DECRQM detection (CSI ? 2026 $ p) with a timeout, notes unsupported terminals ignore the mode, and suggests a BufWriter backend plus Ratatui's diffing so only changed cells are sent.
Recommends Synchronized Output mode 2026, sending CSI ? 2026 h before each frame and CSI ? 2026 l after it so the terminal shows the frame all at once.
States Ratatui's draw() doesn't wrap frames itself and shows code calling crossterm's BeginSynchronizedUpdate/EndSynchronizedUpdate around each draw.
Code ends the update even when draw errors, the answer also sends it from the panic hook and shutdown, and it explains that terminals wait until a timeout otherwise.
Gives DECRQM detection (`\x1b[?2026$p` and the reply codes) and advises one write per frame using Ratatui's diffing, without full clears.
The answer says Enter and Shift+Enter both send `\r` in the traditional encoding, and that telling them apart needs the kitty protocol (CSI u) or xterm's modifyOtherKeys, which it mentions for tmux.

The answer says Bubble Tea v2 requests better key reporting at startup, that terminals like Terminal.app ignore the request and keep sending `\r`, and that tmux flattens Shift+Enter unless extended-keys is configured.
The answer binds alt+enter and ctrl+j, which work in the legacy encoding, plus a backslash-Enter fallback, and calls Shift+Enter 'a nice extra… never the only way'.
The answer watches `tea.KeyboardEnhancementsMsg` and shows 'shift+enter' only when key disambiguation is supported, otherwise 'alt+enter / ctrl+j'.
The answer says both keys send \r in the standard encoding, and it names the kitty keyboard protocol and xterm's modifyOtherKeys as the ways to tell them apart.
The answer says Bubble Tea v2 requests the protocol at startup, that Terminal.app and older terminals send plain \r anyway, and that tmux strips the modifier unless extended-keys is configured.
The answer calls Shift+Enter a 'nice extra' and binds ctrl+j, alt+enter, and backslash continuation as newline keys that work in the legacy encoding.
The answer uses tea.KeyboardEnhancementsMsg to choose between the 'shift+enter: newline' and 'ctrl+j: newline' hints.
The answer says both keys send `\r` (0x0D) in the legacy encoding with no shift bit, and that the kitty keyboard protocol is what lets kitty send a distinct `CSI 13;2u` sequence.

The answer says Bubble Tea v2 requests keyboard enhancements at startup, terminals without support ignore the request and keep sending `\r`, and tmux's extended-keys is off by default, so modifiers are lost.
The answer recommends treating Shift+Enter as a nice extra and always accepting alt+enter, ctrl+j, and a trailing-backslash fallback, all of which work in the legacy encoding.
The answer uses `tea.KeyboardEnhancementsMsg` to set `shiftEnterOK`, and its `newlineHint` shows Shift+Enter only when that is set, otherwise Alt+Enter / Ctrl+J.
The answer says to render the first frame immediately with a best-guess palette and re-theme when the reply arrives, and its startup flow does not block on the query.
The answer recommends DA1 (`ESC [ c`) as a sentinel because replies arrive in order, and keeps a 1–2 s safety timeout for terminals that answer nothing.
The answer enables mode 2031, but on a 997;1n/997;2n report it sets dark/light directly instead of re-querying the background with OSC 11; it re-queries only on focus-in.
The answer turns 2031 off on exit, on SIGTSTP suspend and in the crash handler, but never mentions doing so before handing the terminal to a child process.
The answer says to draw the first frame with a best guess, read replies in the normal input loop, and redraw if the answer differs, so startup never blocks.
The answer sends DA1 right after OSC 11 as an in-order marker so a missing OSC 11 reply is detected immediately, and keeps a 1–2 s safety timeout.
The answer enables mode 2031 but takes the dark/light value from the 997 report directly; it only re-sends OSC 11 on focus-in, not when a 2031 report arrives.
The answer disables 2031 on exit and on SIGTSTP suspend, but never mentions disabling it before handing the terminal to a child process.
Section 2 says to pick an initial theme immediately, draw, then handle the OSC 11 reply as an ordinary input event and redraw if it differs, never blocking startup.
Section 1 sends DA1 right after OSC 11 as a sentinel that almost every terminal answers, and keeps a 1–2s safety timeout as a backstop.
It enables mode 2031 with `ESC [ ? 2031 h`, describes the 997 notifications, and says to re-send OSC 11 when one arrives.
It disables 2031 on exit, including on signals and panics, but never says to turn it off before handing the terminal to a child process.
Sends SetCursorStyle::DefaultUserShape (CSI 0 SP q) in a restore function wired to normal quit, Drop guard, panic hook and signals, and explicitly says ratatui::restore() doesn't handle it.
Presents DefaultUserShape as reliably returning to the user's configured cursor; never mentions that the original shape can't be queried or that xterm treats 0 as a blinking block.
Pushes the title with CSI 22;0 t before setting it and pops with CSI 23;0 t on exit, noting that terminals without stack support ignore it and the title stays stale there.
The answer sends SetCursorStyle::DefaultUserShape (DECSCUSR 0) in restore() on all exit paths, and notes that ratatui::restore() does not touch the cursor shape.
The answer claims code 0 gives back whatever the user configured; it never says the original shape can't be queried or that xterm treats 0 as a blinking block.
The answer uses push (CSI 22;0 t) and pop (CSI 23;0 t), but calls unsupported terminals 'harmless' rather than warning that the old title may be lost there.
The answer recommends SetCursorStyle::DefaultUserShape (DECSCUSR 0) from a restore function called on every exit path, and says ratatui::restore() doesn't touch cursor shape.
The answer says DECSCUSR 0 returns the user's configured shape, but never says the original shape can't be queried or that xterm treats 0 as a blinking block.
The answer pushes the title with CSI 22;0 t before setting it and pops with CSI 23;0 t on exit, and notes unsupporting terminals ignore it, so the title isn't restored there.
